question: What is the difference between internal and external clustering metrics?
options: Internal metrics use only the data and assignments; external metrics compare against known labels
Internal metrics are computed on the training set, external on the test set
explanation: Internal metrics (silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz) need no labels. External metrics (ARI, NMI, purity) need ground truth.

question: Why can't you use plain accuracy to compare cluster labels with true classes?
options: Accuracy is only defined for regression
Cluster ids are arbitrary: cluster 0 may correspond to class 3, so a direct comparison is meaningless
explanation: Clustering metrics must be invariant to permutations of the cluster ids. ARI and NMI work from the contingency table, which ignores naming.

question: A point has silhouette value -0.3. What does that suggest?
options: It sits exactly on the boundary
It is on average closer to another cluster than to its own, so it is probably misassigned
Its cluster has only one point
explanation: s = (b - a) / max(a, b) is negative when a > b, meaning the mean distance to its own cluster exceeds that to the nearest other cluster.

question: Putting every point in its own cluster gives purity 1.0. Which metric correctly reports this as useless?
explanation: ARI subtracts the agreement expected by chance. Singletons never put any pair together, so ARI is 0.

question: On two moons, DBSCAN recovers the true crescents (ARI 1.0) but has a lower silhouette than k-means (ARI 0.24). What does this show?
options: Silhouette should always be preferred over ARI
K-means is the better algorithm for moons
Silhouette rewards compact convex clusters, so it can prefer the wrong answer for non-convex shapes
explanation: Internal metrics encode a notion of good geometry. Long curved clusters have large intra-cluster distances, which silhouette penalizes even when they are correct.

question: For Davies-Bouldin and Calinski-Harabasz, which direction is better?
explanation: Davies-Bouldin measures worst-case overlap between clusters (lower is better). Calinski-Harabasz is a between/within variance ratio (higher is better).
